title: Lecture 7 – Conjunctiva
html:
Source: c7 conjunctiva.pptx – 44 slides

Conjunctiva #1

Diseases #2

  • mainly inflammations
  • Conjunctivitis
  • catarrhal,
  • purulent,
  • pseudomembranous
  • nodular,
  • eruptive

Clearly visible, bright red, distended conjunctival vessels, #3

  • Decreasing toward the limbus of the cornea

1.Catarrhal inflammations #4

  • acute
  • chronic

Acute catarrhal conjunctivitis #5

  • contagious,
  • initially unilateral may become bilateral,
  • epidemics within communities

Acute catarrhal conjunctivitis #6

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • gritty or sandy feeling foreign body sensation
  • dry or wet, sore or tender ocular globe
  • congestion of the conjunctival fornices and tarsal conjunctiva
  • edema chemosis
  • tearing
  • discharge
  • serous (watery)
  • muco-purulent and grossly purulent
  • the eyelids are stuck together on morning
  • punctate corneal infiltrates
  • under the epithelium next to the limbus.

Acute catarrhal conjunctivitis #7

  • Etiology.
  • Koch-Weeks, Morax-Axenfeld Pfeiffer bacteria
  • pneumococcus, streptococcus ,staphylococcus
  • viruses herpes simplex or varicella-herpes
  • ocular burns
  • Management.
  • prophylactical
  • individual and collective hygiene
  • curative
  • astringents (zinc sulfate)
  • Antibiotics broadspectrum locally
  • antibiograme from conjunctival secretion
  • dressing proscribed.

Chronic catarrhal conjunctivitis #8

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • eczematous reaction of the eyelids
  • stickiness
  • hyperemia of the palpebral conjunctiva and conjunctival fornices
  • lacrimal secretion becomes more consistent.

Chronic catarrhal conjunctivitis #9

  • Etiology
  • causes :
  • residual conditions after an acute conjunctivitis
  • incomplete healing the conjunctivitis by Morax-Axenfeld’s bacterium
  • professional diseases
  • dusty, windy and smoky environment from the work place;
  • uncorrected refractive errors.
  • systemic causes
  • diseases of the digestive apparatus and rhinopharynx;
  • dental foci,
  • endocrynological diseases

Chronic catarrhal conjunctivitis #10

  • Management
  • etiological
  • prophylactical
  • removing all kinds of impurities at work place
  • treating all preexisting diseases
  • correction of refractive errors
  • curative
  • astringents and antibiotics drops

2. Purulent inflammations #11

  • gonococcus
  • chlamydia

Gonococcal conjunctivitis Newborn variant #12

  • Particularities
  • bilateral
  • 2-4 days after birth
  • edema, congestion
  • abundant purulent discharge
  • corneea may be involved with ulceration and possible perforation and panophthalmitis
  • purulent inflammation of the whole contents of the eye

Gonococcal conjunctivitis Newborn variant #13

  • Pathogenesis
  • infection
  • before birth by premature rupture of the membranes;
  • during birth by passing the fetus through the moher genitals
  • after birth by contaminated objects.
  • Management
  • prophylactical treatment
  • silver nitrate solution 1% just immediately after birth
  • curative treatment
  • antibiotics topically and systemically.

Gonococcal conjunctivitis Child and adult variant #14

  • Particularities
  • unilateral
  • the same symptoms and signs as by newborn.
  • corneal complications earlier and more severe then in newborn
  • Pathogenesis
  • infected fingers or objects.
  • Management
  • prophylactical
  • proper treatment of infection of the genitals.
  • curative
  • antibiotics topically and systemically

Chlamydial conjunctivitis #15

  • inclusion conjunctivitis of the newborn child.
  • Symptoms and signs
  • within the second week after birth,
  • bilateral
  • the discharge is not so purulent and abundant as in gonococcal conjunctivitis.

Chlamydial conjunctivitis #16

  • Etiology
  • clamydosoon oculogenitalis
  • typical intracellular basophilic inclusion bodies in conjunctival cells
  • scrapings of the tarsal surface of the eyelid,
  • an intermediate phase in the development
  • lives within the epithelium of the mother genitals producing an urethritis and cervicitis
  • conjunctival contamination by delivery

Chlamydial conjunctivitis #17

  • Management
  • tetracyclines,
  • sulphonamides
  • erythromycin
  • locally and systemically.

Slide 18 #18

3. Pseudomembranous inflammations #19

  • diphtheric bacterium
  • pneumococcus, streptococcus.
  • Koch-Weeks bacterium etc.

Diphtherical conjunctivitis #20

  • rare (antidiphthterical vaccinations)
  • children (1-4 years ).

Diphtherical conjunctivitis #21

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • Mild form
  • bilateral
  • membranous exudates grey-whitish upon the conjunctival epithelium
  • easily detach quickly remake.
  • No signs and symptoms of systemic diphtheria
  • localizations at the nose, pharynx or larynx may exist.

Diphtherical conjunctivitis #23

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • Severe form
  • conjunctival chemosis,
  • subconjunctival hemorrhages
  • false membranes
  • detach with difficulty leaving an underlying bleeding conjunctival surface.
  • adenopathies of the surrounding lymph nodes
  • symptoms and signs of systemic diphtheria

Diphtherical conjunctivitis #24

  • Complications.
  • especially within severe form :
  • Corneal infiltrates under epithelium that ulcerates;
  • Cicatricial entropion with trichiasis;
  • Symblepharon
  • adherence between bulbar and palpebral conjunctivae
  • expanding sometimes upon the cornea (ankyloblepharon)
  • Xerosis
  • dryness of the eye (distruction of lacrimal glands).
  • Management.
  • antibiotics (broad spectrum) locally and systemically
  • antidiphtherical serum systemically.

4. Nodular inflammation #25

  • prominent translucent nodules
  • a hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue of the conjunctiva
  • Viral and clamidyal infection
  • two groups
  • acute
  • chronic

4. Nodular inflammation #26

  • Acute nodular form
  • a lot of variants
  • Acute follicular conjunctivitis
  • Swimming bath conjunctivitis

Acute follicular conjunctivitis #27

  • Symptoms and signs
  • initially unilateral,
  • it may become bilateral
  • small red follicles on tarsal and fornical conjunctivae
  • moderate mucous or mucopurulent discharge
  • preauricular adenopathy.
  • Etiology,
  • adenovirus
  • Management
  • antibiotic drops locally

Swimming bath conjunctivitis #28

  • individuals who go to swimming pools
  • also persons who do not
  • incubation of 8-14 days.
  • Symptoms and signs
  • the follicles within the fornices of the conjunctiva
  • moderate conjunctival discharge
  • preauricular adenopathy
  • sometimes involvement of the cornea (superficial punctate keratopathy)

Swimming bath conjunctivitis #29

  • Etiology
  • intracellular inclusions on conjunctival smears stained with Giemsa
  • chlamydosoon oculogenitalis
  • produces also in newborn the inclusion conjunctivitis
  • a subgroup of the chlamydial infections
  • Management
  • astringents, antibiotics and antiseptics
  • topically.

4. Nodular inflammation #30

  • Chronic nodular forms
  • trachoma
  • vernal conjunctivitis

Trachoma( granulomatous conjunctivitis), #31

  • follicles, that invade the cornea and tends to cure by development of cicatricial tissue.

Trachoma( granulomatous conjunctivitis), #32

  • Simptoms and signs.
  • a) initial or dubious trachoma
  • unilateral hypertrophy of the papillae within the conjunctiva
  • prominent follicles upon superior tarsal conjunctiva having a milky appearance
  • other associated conjunctival inflammations
  • (Koch-Weeks’bacterium)
  • intracellular inclusions on the conjunctival smears
  • (similar to inclusion and swimming bath conjunctivitis)

Trachoma #33

  • Simptoms and signs.
  • b) florid or real trachoma.
  • follicles become larger, numerous, opalescent and break under light pressure.
  • the cornea is invaded by a superficial vasculo granulomatous tissue (pannus),
  • like a curtain expands from the superior limbus downwards.
  • tarsal plate become infiltrated
  • ptosis.
  • intracellular inclusions in the conjunctival smears

Trachoma #34

  • Simptoms and signs.
  • c) precicatricial trachoma
  • follicles in differeing evolution stages
  • conjunctival scars;
  • d) cicatricial trachoma
  • complications :
  • Corneal ulcerations at the level of the pannus;
  • Entropion with trichiasis
  • Symblepharon ;
  • Conjunctival xerosis
  • destruction of the lacrimal glands

Trachoma #35

  • Etiology.
  • chlamydozoon trachomatis
  • subgroup of chlamydial infections.
  • Management
  • prophylactical
  • better hygiene for individuals and communities
  • ontagious
  • curative therapy
  • antibiotics and sulfonamides topically and systemically

Vernal conjunctivitis (spring catarrh) #36

  • bilateral and affects mostly men.
  • The duration is 5-6 years
  • recurrences during warm seasons (spring, summer)
  • alleviation or disappearance during the cold seasons (winter, fall).
  • cures without sequelae
  • Simptoms and signs
  • Itching
  • photophobia
  • watery stringy discharge.

Vernal conjunctivitis (spring catarrh) forms #37

  • a)Palpebral or tarsal
  • pink excrescences at the upper tarsal conjunctiva separated by ditches
  • Similar to large cobblestones or crocodile skin;

Vernal conjunctivitis (spring catarrh) forms #38

  • b) Limbal
  • a hypertrophy of the perilimbal conjunctiva
  • prominent grey-yellowish, translucent ring with a hard consistence;
  • c) Mixed
  • the signs above.

Vernal conjunctivitis #39

  • Etiology.
  • allergic reaction to the sun radiations
  • Treatment
  • cotricosteroids and antihistamines locally and systemically
  • itching
  • drops with weak acetic acid solution
  • calcium, B and C vitamins systemically.

5. Eruptive inflammation #40

  • during the evolution of some infectious disease
  • measles,
  • varicella etc.
  • phlyctenular conjunctivitis

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis #41

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • Benign form
  • phlyctenules at the corneoscleral junction.
  • light prominent nodules
  • the size of a pin’s head
  • triangular area of conjunctival hyperemia
  • the top at the phlyctenule
  • the basis towards the conjunctival fornice.
  • cycle
  • grows within a week then ulcerated and eventually disappears

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis #42

  • Symptoms and signs.
  • Severe form
  • Corneal phlyctenule
  • a nodular infiltration under the Bowmann’s membrane;
  • Phlyctenular ulceration of the cornea
  • arisen from a limbal phlyctenule;
  • Eczematous pannus
  • a vasculo-granulomatous tissue invading superficially the cornea all around the limbus

Phlyctenular conjunctivitis #43

  • Etiology.
  • Mostly an allergic manifestation of tuberculosis
  • Management
  • antiseptics, astringents and mydriatics locally
  • systemic treatment of tuberculosis or its sequelae

Diphtheria #44

  • Sore throat fever.
  • grey or white patch develops in the throat.
  • can block the airway and create a barking cough as in croup.
  • The neck may swell due to enlarged lymph nodes
  • Complications
  • myocarditis, inflammation of nerves (paralysis),
  • kidney problems,
  • bleeding  (low levels of platelets).
